newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Feb 28.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Feb 28.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW
The U.S. is expected to be irritated by Australia's rebuff to its request to co-sponsor a tough anti-China resolution at next month's Geneva meeting of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights.

Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer has not yet made a final decision but accepts Australia's trade interests requires an extremely cautious approach to the tough line being pursued by Washington. Australia already irritated the US by opposing the extraterritorial application of U.S. legislation limiting trade with Iran and Cuba, and the move by Australia to distance itself from the US could undermine the Federal Government's efforts to build closer relations with Washington. Page 1.

The Victorian Supreme Court heard yesterday that former chief executive officer for Coles Myer, Brian Quinn, had organised the retail company to oversee renovations on a second property in the Victorian Bayside peninsula suburb of Mt Eliza, which generated more than A$2 million in charges, claiming he and the company were overcharged on the property. Quinn is facing trial on allegations the costs of A$4.5 million worth of renovations on his Templestowe home between 1982 and 1988 were concealed in a conspiracy between Quinn and Coles' former maintenance manager, Graham Lanyon.

Six Aboriginal claimants who have refused to agree to the A$1.1 billion Century zinc mine will meet with the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission today in an effort to end the native title impasse. The claimants have effectively refused an offer from Century Zinc and the Queensland Government under which their communities would reap more than A$3.5 million. The Waanyi and Maingginda communities have already agreed to Century's offer but require signatures from the remaining claimants. Page 3

Despite reporting a slight drop in capital spending in the last three months of 1996, companies plan to boost investment over the rest of the financial year, with estimates from the Australian Bureau of Statistics putting business investments at $43 billion in 1996-97, based on actual expenditure in the first half of the year and expectations for the second half. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Australia's health ministers have warned the Federal Government of a health crisis by 2010 unless major reforms are implemented to cut demand for public hospitals and boost funding for health services. The fears were raised at a special meeting of Health Ministers as all Government's conceded that they have failed to provide enough funds to match increasing community demand for health services. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard yesterday rejected claims by Victorian Premier, Jeff Kennett, that Federal Government incentives to move people onto private health insurance was "money down the drain". Standing by the Coalition's health policy, Howard seized on comments made by Kennett last September that the health initiative was "long overdue". Page 2.

The heat remains on Independent Senator Mal Colston after a Government inquiry found he may have abused guidelines on parliamentary perks. Following initial investigations, Administrative Services Minister David Jull said there might be irregularities in Senator Colston's use of Comcar in Canberra and his use of hire cars elsewhere. Jull said that a full investigation into the Senator would continue. Page 1.

Australia's top air safety regulator and Civil Aviation Safety Authority board member, Leroy Keith, yesterday accused CASA chairman-hopeful, Dick Smith, of alarming air travellers with untrue statements concerning safety and has warned the Federal Government he will resign if a hands-on chairman is appointed to CASA. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The Chief Justice of the High Court has accused Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer of threatening the stability of society with his vocal attacks and long-term campaign against the court's Wik judgement. In a private letter to Fischer, Sir Gerard Brennenwarned that the public attacks were damaging and undermining public confidence in the court. Page 1.

Federal Treasurer Peter Costello has warned there will not be much change in unemployment levels without a further freeing up of the labour market. In an interview, Costello made it clear that industrial relations reforms just passed by the Senate, will not substantially reduce unemployment. For jobless levels to fall, he says there needs to be flexibility for wages to go lower as well as higher. Page 1.

Senior officials of the Australian Medical Association have backed away from the ailing private health insurance industry, instead urging patients to forget health cover and pay for their own expenses from their own pockets. The AMA's economics committee eleased evidence revealing most patients would be better off financially if they took such an approach. Today the Federal Government is being presented with recommendations of an inquiry into health funds. Page 1.

In a move which could have major implications on Australia's tertiary sector, school-leavers who miss out on a place at the University of Technology, Sydney, because of an insufficient entrance ranking will be able to buy their way into some courses from next year. Up to a quarter of all undergraduate places would be offered to students who are willing to pay the full cost of their degree - expected to average about A$50,000 Page 3.
THE AGE

Prime Minister John Howard and Treasurer Peter Costello have hit back at Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett's criticism of the Federal Government's health policy which provides incentives for private health insurance. Howard reaffirmed the health policy and evn quoted Kennett, who last September said the reforms were "long overdue".
Page A1.

It has been revealed that the Prime Minister of Papua New Guinea, Sir Julius Chan, and his family are major shareholders in a security company which is operated by two Australians accused of hiring Australian police and former anti-terrorist soldiers to wrk in PNG. Investigations reveal the recruits were brought in to the island nation to settle life-threatening disputes in two secret operations late last year and early this year. Page A1.

Under a radical proposal to slash the nation's greenhouse emissions, Australians who drive big cars with high fuel consumption could face higher registration fees. The committee charged with preparing a strategy to reduce Australia's contribution to global warming has also recommended a series of measures, including the introduction of tolls, to discourage private car usage in cities. Page A1.

As Victoria's industrial unrest continues, more than 4080 teachers have voted to step up a campaign against the Kennett Government's Budget cuts. Meanwhile, public transport staff are threatening industrial action next week to disrupt the Melbourne Grand rix and emergency service workers are also considering strike action if the State Government maintains its fiscal squeeze and privatisation plans.
Page A1.
